Immune System
The immune system is composed of the innate immune system and the acquired
immune system. Innate immunity involves the body’s physical barriers (skin and mucous
membranes) and nonspecific immune defenses, including phagocytes, natural killer cells,
cytokines, and complement factors.1 Natural killer cells are important in immune
defense against viral pathogens, accounting for spontaneous cytolytic activity toward
cells infected with pathogens.1,2 Macrophages are responsible for a number of immune
activities, including presentation of antigens to lymphocytes, phagocytosis of foreign
particles, and production of cytokines. Neutrophils play a key role in the phagocytosis of
bacterial and viral pathogens and the release of important cytokines.2 Cytokines and
complement factors are important for communication with and activation of the
acquired immune system. The acquired immune system, made up of T and B
lymphocytes and plasma-secreted antibodies, provides a more specific immune
response.1

Exercise
Exercise leads to a variety of changes within the body and immune system. As exertion
increases, breathing switches from primarily nasal to mouth breathing. As a result, the
lower respiratory tract experiences increased exposure to infectious particles. In
addition, the respiratory mucosa begins to experience a cooling and drying effect as part
of this switch, slowing ciliary movement and increasing mucous viscosity, which decrease
overall mucociliary clearing.1

Innate immune system activity fluctuates with exercise. Acute high-intensity exercise
lasting less than 1 hour results in an increase in natural killer cell count and macrophage
count and function. This acute increase in natural killer cell count falls below pre-
exercise levels within approximately 30 minutes of cessation of the activity. Intense
exercise lasting more than 1 hour does not lead to the same rise in natural killer cell
activity and results in a larger and longer drop in natural killer cell activity as the athlete
recovers. Proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines increase in response to
acute exercise. Neutrophils exhibit a variable response to activity; moderate activity
results in an increase in the number of neutrophils. However, intense exercise appears
to suppress their oxidative activity.2
Similar to the innate immune response, the acquired immune system demonstrates
variability with exercise. Acute and moderate exercise lead to a general increase in
lymphocyte counts. However, with more intense exercise, the lymphocyte count and B-
cell function decrease. Antibody production, most specifically IgA, also exhibits
impairment with prolonged exercise.1,2 The ratio of CD4+ to CD8+ cells, part of the
acquired immune response, is important for cellular immunity. This ratio decreases with
heavy or intense exercise. A decrease in CD4+ count also leads to decreased cytokine
output, which then affects communication with natural killer cells, macrophages, and B-
cell proliferation.2
The open window effect is the term commonly used to describe a time frame following
acute intense exercise in which a brief period of immunosuppression occurs. This
immunosuppression is a combined effect of decreased activity of the innate and
acquired immune systems, including decreased mucociliary clearance, decreased
natural killer cell and macrophage count and activity, decreased mucosal IgA and T
lymphocyte count, and a decreased CD4+:CD8+ ratio. This is seen as an open window in
which the athlete is more susceptible to infection, often upper respiratory infection.1,2
Compared with a sedentary lifestyle, moderate exercise has demonstrated a reduced
risk of infection, whereas intense exercise appears to result in the open window effect,
potentially increasing the risk of infection for a brief period.2

Not surprisingly, infection generally has a negative effect on athletic performance. Acute
illness decreases muscle activity while increasing cardiopulmonary effort. These effects
usually are minimal with mild illnesses, but the risk for harm still exists.1
Because many elite athletes may face periods of heavy or intense exercise in preparation
for competition, steps can be taken to maximize their health and well-being to minimize
the risk of infection. These steps include ensuring that the athlete is getting proper
nutrition and regular and appropriate sleep, avoiding overtraining, and minimizing other
life stressors. Proper hand hygiene and avoiding touching the face and nose help reduce
the risk of infection. Avoiding large crowds or individuals with known illness also is
important.2

Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Types 1 and 2
HSV types 1 and 2 are viral infections commonly observed in athletes and the general
population. Historically, HSV type 2 was associated solely with genital herpes infection.
However, crossover has been noted between the HSV infection types and the location of
infection on the body.3 HSV is transmitted through direct skin contact and can occur in a
variety of locations (face, lips, neck, shoulders).1,4-6 Herpes gladiatorum and herpes
rugbiorum commonly occur in wrestlers and rugby players. Most often, this type of
infection is associated with HSV-1.5 Because of the direct exposure and contact
associated with wrestling and rugby, the head and neck are most commonly affected in
this population, occurring in about 71.9% of patients.7 Other common skin locations
include the extremities (42%) and trunk (28%).4,7 Herpetic whitlow, an infection occurring
on the finger or thumb, may be another presentation. Herpes labialis (cold sores), which
affects the lips or perioral area, can be transmitted through sharing water bottles or
other equipment that may be in direct contact with the mouth. Herpes labialis can
manifest as reactivation resulting from cold or ultraviolet light stress and commonly
develops in skiers.4 Herpes conjunctivitis and blepharitis also have been reported but

are not common.4 Outbreaks associated with HSV have shut down various athletic

After exposure, an incubation period between 2 and 14 days occurs before vesicles
appear.3 The mean incubation period is between 5.1 and 8.5 days.4,7 During this time,
asymptomatic viral shedding may occur. Symptomatic recurrent infections generally
demonstrate a shorter time frame for shedding the virus, lasting approximately 3 to 4
days.3 Lesions often rupture and crust over after 5 to 7 days of their onset and can last
as long as 2 to 3 weeks.1 Primary HSV infections may present with a prodrome of
systemic symptoms, including low-grade fever, malaise, sore throat, and
lymphadenopathy. Within a couple of days, painful, grouped vesicles appear, often
coalescing.5 Diagnosis of HSV often is clinical, but a low threshold of diagnostic
uncertainty should exist before considering microbiologic testing, because herpes
gladiatorum is commonly misdiagnosed or confused with other skin infections.5,9,10 PCR
assays are the preferred testing method because of increased sensitivity compared with
other modalities, such as culture or Tzanck smear.
Athletes with an HSV infection should not participate in any contact activities or share
equipment until the infection has cleared. Treatment decisions should be based on
clinical suspicion. Oral valacyclovir is commonly recommended.3 Topical antiviral agents
have not been shown to be effective. Medications should be initiated as soon as possible
for herpes gladiatorum and rugbiorum because the sooner treatment is started, the
more effective it will be. If medications are administered within 24 hours of the onset of
symptoms, the time until PCR clearance is lessened in adolescents with recurrent herpes
gladiatorium.3,4 Care must be taken with lesions near the eye because they can progress
to herpetic conjunctivitis, keratitis, and ulceration. Herpes labialis often is self-limited,
but treatment started within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms may limit their
duration.1
Return-to-play decisions vary depending on the level of competition (high school versus
college) and whether the athlete has systemic symptoms (more common in primary
infections) or no systemic symptoms. In general, return to play may be considered if the
athlete has been receiving antiviral medications for 120 hours and lesions are scabbed

72 hours, and no systemic symptoms are present. The National Federation of State High
School Associations (NFHS) recommends that for athletes with a primary HSV infection,
all lesions must be scabbed over, no new lesions have appeared in 48 hours or more,
and the athlete has been receiving antiviral treatment for at least 10 days for an
infection involving skin lesions only or 14 days or more for an infection with associated
systemic symptoms before returning to play.5
Evidence shows that nucleoside analogues (valacyclovir) are helpful in suppressing
recurrent outbreaks. Therefore, in athletes with known recurrent HSV infections,
antiviral prophylaxis or suppressive therapy should be considered.4,5,11 Prophylactic
treatment should be initiated approximately 5 days before the season, camp, or
tournament to ensure that proper drug levels are attained before competition. One
study reported that approximately 30% of high school wrestlers were infected or
colonized with HSV; however, only 3% were aware that they carried the virus.12 Skin
checks are commonly used in wrestling to identify infectious lesions before competition.
Exclusion of athletes with an active HSV infection from competition is important in
preventing outbreaks.3,4 Although many studies have demonstrated that fomites are not
a substantial contributor to the spread of HSV infection,5,7 avoiding equipment sharing
and properly cleaning equipment between uses is a good general practice.

Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)
VZV is another virus in the herpes family of viruses. Primary infection with VZV manifests
as varicella or chickenpox. Transmission may be airborne or via skin-to-skin
transmission. Airborne transmission of varicella is increasingly rare in the era of
immunization.4 VZV presents as a vesicular rash on an erythematous base and often
appears to be in various stages, with some lesions being vesicular and others crusted.
Primary infection with VZV is self-limited, but after resolution of symptoms it lies
dormant in the dorsal spinal root ganglion. Shingles is caused by reactivation of VZV,
often after stress or illness.3 Shingles presents as a similar vesicular rash but follows a
single unilateral dermatome (Figure 1). The diagnosis of chickenpox and shingles is
made based on the clinical presentation. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, the diagnosis
can be confirmed via PCR of vesicular fluid, or VZV culture can be performed.3 Treatment
often is not necessary for young healthy athletes who may display primary VZV infection.
However, oral valacyclovir or acyclovir may be considered for patients with primary VZV
infection (chickenpox) who are at risk of moderate to severe disease, patients with
primary infection who are older than 12 years, patients with chronic cutaneous or
pulmonary disorders, and patients being treated with short-term intermittent or
aerosolized corticosteroids.3,4
Return-to-play decisions depend on the level of competition (high school versus college)
and the type of infection. In general, athletes with VZV infections should be excluded
from participation until all lesions are scabbed over or have an adherent scab and no
new lesions have appeared for 48 hours.4,13 However, the NFHS recommends that
athletes with primary VZV infection complete 10 to 14 days of oral antiviral treatment

Poxvirus
Derived from the Poxviridae family, molluscum contagiosum primarily affects the youth
athlete, with the highest incidence of infection occurring in athletes younger than 14
years.4,5,14 It is more commonly seen in athletes participating in swimming, gymnastics,
and wrestling. The virus is transmitted via direct skin-to-skin contact and can be spread
via sexual contact or fomites (eg, towels).3,5,14 Molluscum contagiosum presents as a 2-
to 5-mm localized pearly or flesh-colored papule with central umbilication (Figure 2). In
general, no associated erythema and no lymphadenopathy or other systemic symptoms
are present. Lesions often are found on the face and/or extremities but can occur in the
genital region. Patients generally are asymptomatic, but a secondary bacterial infection
can develop. The diagnosis is made by observing the characteristic appearance of the
rash. The infection often is self-limited but may take months to years to fully resolve.3 No
therapy is especially effective but should be considered for athletes participating in
contact sports. Management is with 10% potassium hydroxide, cryotherapy, or
curettage, which is recommended by some institutions before athletes can return to
play.4,5 Cantharidin and imiquimod have demonstrated minimal-to-no added benefit.4 If
only a single lesion is present or the infection is localized, the infected area can be
covered so the athlete can return to activity.

Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
HPV is a common infection manifesting as the common wart. It is transmitted primarily
via direct skin-to-skin contact. Fomites, such as public showers or shared equipment and
towels, have been reported to be potential risk factors for transmission of HPV.1,4,15
Warts present as hyperkeratotic papules that do not retain the papillary ridges of skin.
The diagnosis of HPV is clinical. Skin warts often are painless and commonly present in
groups. They can occur in any location on the body but commonly develop on hands and
feet and around or under nails. The characteristic appearance of thrombosed epithelial
vessels—little black dots—within a wart help to distinguish it from other common skin
lesions, such as calluses or corns.3,4 Although spontaneous regression will occur with
many skin warts, the time for regression may vary between 6 months and 2 years.3,4
Multiple treatment options are available, including topical medications to removal via
curettage, are aimed at physical destruction of the epithelial skin. Topical management

Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)/Methicillin-
Sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA)
S aureus is responsible for approximately 80% of bacterial skin infections.1 Nasal
colonization with S aureus is variable, with reports in the literature ranging between 12%
and 30%.17 MRSA colonization similarly has variable rates, with studies reporting
colonization ranging from 4% to 23% in athletes. Colonization rates seem to peak during
times of highest activity (ie, midseason). Colonization does appear to increase the risk of
infection, estimated as a sevenfold increase.18 However, despite higher rates of
colonization, colonization alone does not appear to correlate well with outbreaks.4,17
Braun et al reported a community-acquired MRSA infection rate of approximately 0.15%

Superficial fungal infections are often caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi in the
Trichophyton and Microsporum genera.3 Transmission occurs via direct skin contact or
via fomites. Contact sports, such as wrestling and judo, are associated with the highest

Influenza
Influenza commonly occurs during the winter months, which span from November to
April in the northern hemisphere and April to October in the southern hemisphere.
Three types of influenza viruses exist: A, B, and C. However, type C tends to result in
fairly mild disease and generally is not responsible for epidemic or pandemic
outbreaks.3 Influenza types A and B may vary from year to year because of antigenic
drift.3
The diagnosis can be made clinically with the presentation of high fever, malaise,
myalgia, and upper respiratory tract illness during the typical flu season. A rapid
molecular test can be used to confirm the diagnosis and help direct therapy.
Management is with neuraminidase inhibitors (eg, oseltamivir, zanamivir, and peramivir)
and more recently via a selective inhibitory or an influenza co-dependent endonuclease,
baloxavir.3 Management is most effective if initiated within the first 48 hours. Overall,
seasonal immunization is the best method for preventing infection during influenza
season.3,4 Return to play for athletes infected with influenza should be guided by their
tolerance for activity after resolution of fever and improvement in respiratory symptoms.
Those receiving treatment via a neuraminidase inhibitor should complete 5 days of
therapy before returning to play.4

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)
Mononucleosis is a viral infection caused by EBV. Its prevalence is highest in adolescence
and early adulthood, with 1% to 3% of college students infected each year.1 It is
estimated that approximately 90% of adults have been infected; however, most
individuals are unaware they were ever infected.3,32 Humans are the only known
reservoir, with transmission occurring via respiratory and oral secretions.3 Therefore,
infection in group and team settings with close contact is common.
After exposure, the incubation period is between 30 and 50 days before symptom onset.
Symptoms of mononucleosis include fatigue, severe sore throat, malaise, headache, and
fever.3,32 Physical examination findings include exudative pharyngitis
(approximately80%), lymphadenopathy (classically posterior cervical chain),
splenomegaly (50% to 100%), palatal petechiae (25%), and/or a diffuse rash (10% to 40%).
The rash classically occurs in patients who have received amoxicillin or ampicillin
treatment for pharyngitis. This rash does not represent an allergy.32,33 The diagnosis is
commonly made based on Hoagland criteria; a history of fever, pharyngitis, or
lymphadenopathy; 50% or more lymphocytes with at least 10% atypical lymphocytes in a

Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)
SARS-CoV-2 was labeled a global pandemic by the World Health Organization on March

and the postponement or truncation of professional and college sports. The novel
coronavirus is a member of the nidovirus family and is transmitted from human to
human via respiratory droplets, but it also can be contracted from bats.40 The virus has
an affinity for the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptor, which is highly expressed
in the lower respiratory tract. SARS-CoV-2 gains access to multiple organ systems in
which angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 is expressed, including the lungs, heart, kidney,

Bordetella Pertussis
Pertussis (whooping cough) is a respiratory illness caused by B pertussis. With the
introduction of the pertussis vaccine, adolescents and adults currently are those most
affected. Pertussis presents in three phases. The first is the catarrhal phase. The patient
has generalized malaise, rhinorrhea, and mild cough with or without fever. Pertussis
often is overlooked at this phase because of its resemblance to viral illnesses. The next
phase is the paroxysmal phase, which usually begins around the second week of illness
and is characterized by a severe rapid paroxysmal cough. The cough often is followed by
an inspiratory whoop, which is what gives pertussis its name. Posttussive vomiting also is
a common feature of this phase of illness and may last for 2 to 3 months if unmanaged
before progressing to the convalescent phase. In the convalescent phase, the patient
experiences a gradual improvement in the severity of the cough.3
The diagnosis of pertussis is made via culture or PCR; although culture has been
considered the criterion standard, it is less optimal because of the fastidious nature of
the organism.3 Management via azithromycin does not need to be delayed while
awaiting laboratory results. The goal of management is to decrease the duration of
symptoms and to prevent additional spread. Athletes infected by B pertussis should be
excluded from close contact until they have completed 5 days of appropriate antibiotic
therapy or until 3 weeks have elapsed since the onset of cough.3,38,52 A diphtheria,
tetanus acellular, and pertussis booster is recommended every 10 years after the
primary immunization series.

Meningitis
Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, which surround the brain and spinal cord.
Multiple causes of meningitis exist, but the most common causes are viral and bacterial.
Bacterial meningitis is of greatest concern because of its increased morbidity and
mortality, even with appropriate therapy.20,55
Although the symptoms of viral and bacterial meningitis are similar, the onset of
bacterial meningitis usually is more rapid, sometimes occurring over a period of hours.55
Nausea, vomiting, photophobia, malaise, and drowsiness are observed with both types.
The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status is more commonly
observed in bacterial cases, with 44% of patients having all three symptoms. As the
illness progresses, meningeal signs, such as the Kernig sign (inability to straighten the leg
with the hip flexed) and the Brudzinski sign (forward neck flexion causes knee or hip
flexion), may become evident.20 The patient also may be lethargic or irritable on physical
examination.55 Dissemination of the bacterial infection may lead to Waterhouse-
Friderichsen syndrome or hemorrhage of the adrenal glands, which may result in
purpura, shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and organ failure.56
Common viral causes of meningitis are enteroviruses, such as echovirus and coxsackie
virus. These viruses usually are spread via respiratory secretions or via fecal-oral contact.

bacterial meningitis.55N meningitidis is an important cause of bacterial meningitis

must be assumed until proven otherwise. A lumbar puncture should be obtained unless

N Gonorrhoeae
Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted illness caused by the bacteria N gonorrhoeae. It is
the second most common cause of bacterial STI in the world. Women most commonly
present with infections of the cervix and complaints of vaginal discharge, dysuria, or
pelvic pain. More than 50% of women may be asymptomatic, and unmanaged infection
can ascend the urogenital tract, causing salpingitis and pelvic inflammatory disease. This
may lead to increased morbidity because of ectopic pregnancy.58 Infection also can
disseminate to other areas of the body, causing skin and synovial infection.20 Men, more
commonly than women, present with symptoms of gonorrheal infection, including
urethritis, urethral discharge, and testicular pain. To confirm the diagnosis, nucleic acid
amplification testing can be performed from urine, cervical, or urethral swabbing.
Empiric therapy should be administered based on a patient’s history and clinical
examination findings. Dual therapy via a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone and a
single dose of azithromycin administered concurrently is recommended for
uncomplicated gonococcal infections.3 Complicated infections, such as pelvic
inflammatory disease and epididymitis, should be managed via ceftriaxone in
combination with doxycycline for 14 days.3,58 Athletes should refrain from sexual activity
until treatment is completed.

Syphilis
Syphilis is caused by the spirochete T pallidum. There are 17.7 million infections
worldwide, with cases increasing yearly in the United States.60 Infection is acquired via
direct contact with an infectious lesion during sex. Spirochetes directly penetrate
mucous membranes or enter through abrasions in the skin. Transmission also can occur
vertically during pregnancy.60 Painless chancres at the site of infection with surrounding
lymphadenopathy are the characteristic finding of primary infection and occur 10 to 90
days after exposure. They usually are located on the glans, labia, and perineum.

exposure. Tertiary syphilis develops 1 to 46 years after exposure, and infection involves
the cardiovascular system (aortitis) and granulomatous disease of the skin,
subcutaneous tissues, bones, and viscera. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage of
infection and can present with meningitis, stroke, vision and hearing loss, dementia, and
tabes dorsalis.

treponemal tests, such as fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption. Treponemal
testing usually becomes reactive within 2 weeks of chancre development, but rapid

develop. Management of syphilis depends on the stage of disease at presentation.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus
HIV is an enveloped retrovirus that is acquired via sexual intercourse, contaminated
blood, or perinatal transmission (Resource 2). Approximately 37 million people are
estimated to be living with HIV worldwide.62 HIV attaches to CD4 and CCR5 and fuses
with the cell membrane. Primary infection occurs 4 to 10 weeks after infection and
presents as a flu-like illness, with fever, joint pain, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.63
These symptoms are followed by an asymptomatic period that can last months to years.
During this period, HIV replicates in CD4 cells. As the CD4 cell count drops, opportunistic
infections, such as P carinii, Kaposi sarcoma, cytomegalovirus, and cryptosporidium,
signify immunosuppression and the development of AIDS.1 The threshold for HIV testing
should be low, especially if a high degree of clinical suspicion exists. The timing of testing
is important because HIV antibodies may take 3 months to develop.1
The goals of HIV management are to suppress HIV replication and improve cellular
immunity. This is done via antiretroviral medications in a variety of combinations that
are referred to as highly active antiretroviral therapy. Antiretroviral drugs include
nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non-nucleoside/nucleotide
reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, and CCR5 inhibitors. All athletes
infected with HIV should receive highly active antiretroviral therapy regardless of CD4
count, and treatment should continue for life.63
